life.title: Its life
life.q: It passed every check. Will it still work in year {life}?
life.signed: It was signed off as a perfect design: a typical chip, at room temperature, on a clean supply, brand new. Out here, none of that lasts.
life.phone.story: {fleet} phones, {life} years, up to {tMax} °C. It must be cheap and fast: a phone that crashes comes back, but nobody keeps one for long.
life.car.story: {fleet} cars, {life} years, from freezing winters to {tMax} °C near the engine. A car carries hundreds of chips, so car makers count bad ones in parts per million.
life.datacentre.story: {fleet} chips running flat out, hot all day, for {life} years. Across a fleet this big, radiation flips a bit that matters about {perDay} times a day.
life.chart: Share of the chips shipped that have failed, year by year, by cause
life.cause.timing.d: Passed the factory's Test, then miss the clock: hot, when the supply dips under load, and as the transistors age.
life.cause.escape.d: Broken chips the test patterns did not catch. They fail almost at once.
life.cause.weak.d: Hidden flaws that pass every test, then break in the first months of use.
life.cause.wear.d: Current slowly pushes metal atoms along a wire until it breaks (electromigration).
life.req.silent: Silent wrong answers a year, across them all
life.req.cost: Cost of a good chip, against the plan
life.yield: Chips that pass the factory's Test: {v}%.
life.speed: Signed off at {mhz} MHz; sold at {sold} MHz.
life.hint.typical: Most chips fail at the factory's Test. The perfect design assumed a typical chip, and half of all chips are slower than typical. Sell it slower than it was signed off (margin).
life.hint.field: Chips pass the Test, then fail out here: hot, with the supply dipping, ageing. Testing hot at a low supply catches them at the factory instead; margin and a stronger power grid leave them room.
life.hint.escape: Broken chips slip through the Test. Your test patterns catch {cov}% of the faults they are graded on; a design whose patterns catch more lets fewer through, and testing hot catches some the patterns miss.
life.hint.weak: Weak chips pass the Test and break in their first months. Burn-in runs every chip hot for hours before it ships, so the weak ones break in the factory.
life.hint.weakBurnt: Weak chips still get through burn-in. A hot test that rejects chips unlike their neighbours screens more, and every extra copy of logic is more area where a flaw can hide.
life.hint.wear: The wires are wearing out: this chip works too hot for too long. Wider wires, a lower voltage or better cooling are what people try.
life.hint.silent: Radiation flips stored bits, and nobody notices the wrong answer. Error-correcting memory finds and fixes almost all of them.
life.hint.silentLogic: The memory is protected, but a flipped bit in the logic still gives a wrong answer nobody sees. A second copy of the logic that checks the first (lockstep) catches it, at a cost in area.
life.hint.perf: Too slow for this customer: the margin you added costs speed. A stronger power grid and a hot test can stand in for some of it.
life.hint.cost: Too expensive for this customer: every protection costs area, test time or chips thrown away. Which does this place not need?
life.hint.ok: It ships: every need here is met. Could it be cheaper or faster without breaking one? Would the same choices work in the other places?
life.margin: Margin: sold slower than signed off
life.hot: Test hot, at a low supply
life.model: A textbook model, simplified, from the earlier site: the direction and rough size of each effect matter, not the digits. Your design brings its test patterns and its slowest path.
life.notYet: Your design is not right yet. A wrong design fails everywhere; this is the life it would have once it is right.
life.teaser: Passing every check means it is right at the conditions it was checked at. Then it is made, tested and shipped, and lives for years somewhere hot, shaken and far from typical.

xray.title: X-ray
xray.q: What is this chip for? A photo of its die tells you, if you can read it.
xray.on: See it as a die photo
xray.type.core.clue: A tile of fine, irregular logic with a small regular grid of cache beside it, often copied several times.
xray.type.gpu.clue: Many identical small units in rows: one tile, copied again and again.
xray.type.npu.clue: A dense square array of identical multiply units, with memory close beside it.
xray.type.logic.clue: A fine, noise-like texture with no pattern: thousands to millions of gates, placed by software.
xray.type.cache.clue: A perfectly regular grid: the same memory cell, repeated millions of times.
xray.type.flash.clue: A coarser regular grid of bigger cells: memory that keeps its contents with the power off.
xray.type.phy.clue: Striped strips along an edge: the interfaces to memory chips or to other chips.
xray.type.analog.clue: A few large, irregular shapes and round coils: circuits drawn by hand, for clocks, power and signals from the real world.
xray.type.io.clue: Rows of squares around the edge, where wires join the die to its package.
xray.read.chip: An AI chip: most of it is copies of one compute tile, with memory and wide links to the memory chips beside it. Often what limits it is how fast data arrives, not how fast it computes.
xray.read.soc: A phone's chip: a whole computer on one die, a district for each job (cores, graphics, AI, the camera), all sharing one memory, all inside a small, cool package.
xray.read.mcu: A car's microcontroller: small cores in step, a big block of flash that keeps its program, and hand-drawn circuits that sense and steer the real world. Built to last, not to be fast.
xray.find: Find this in the picture, and tap it: {type}.
xray.done: You can read this die: every kind of block on it is found.

chip.fed: Memory keeps its cores fed: they get {work}× the starting chip's work done.
chip.starved: Its cores could do {peak}× the starting chip's work, but they wait for numbers from memory {idle}% of the time, so they do {work}×: the memory wall.
chip.reuse.label: Reuse: how often each number fetched is used
chip.reuse.notice: Every number the cores work on comes from memory, over wires. Used many times once it has arrived (kept close, in the chip's own memory, or shared by many requests at once), it asks less of the wires and of the energy. But not every job can reuse its numbers. Which kinds can?

chip.mem.names: memory stacked beside it, in its package
chip.mem.notice: Memory stacked right beside the chip, in the same package, sends numbers many times faster and spends less energy on each one. It also costs more, is harder to make and holds less. When is it worth it?

floor.title: The floor
floor.q: How far is your chip from what physics allows?
floor.energy: Erasing one bit of information costs at least kT ln 2 (Landauer's limit): about {zj} zeptojoules at room temperature. Ordinary logic erases bits all the time, so this is the floor under every step.
floor.yours: Your chip spends about {times} times the floor on each multiply-add: its arithmetic alone is {math} times, and {moving}% of the energy goes to fetching numbers. Physics leaves a lot of room. What stands in the way is engineering.
floor.room: At room temperature, the floor is as above. A colder chip has a lower one: try it.
floor.cold: At {k} K, the chip's floor is {pct}% of the room's. But its heat must be pumped out to the room, and even a perfect refrigerator spends {pump}% of the total doing it: exactly the room's floor again. Real refrigerators do worse. Cooling cannot lower the floor; it can make real switches waste less, which is the bet of superconducting logic.
floor.speed: At your clock ({ghz} billion ticks a second in this model), light in glass travels about {cm} cm in one tick. Your chip is {mm} mm corner to corner: at least {ticks} of a tick to cross. Real wires are many times slower than light, so the slowest signal must cross far less.
floor.aim: Ways that aim at the floor:
floor.model: From the earlier site's physics floor: first principles, with your chip's energy from the 45 nm table it already uses. The count of bits a multiply-add erases is an estimate of its order of magnitude.
clk.ladderK: Time at every length, tenfold at each step
clk.ladderAria: One scale of time, from trillionths of a second to fifty years, with marks from the lab's engines
clk.m.path: a full adder's slowest path: {ps} ps
clk.m.factory: a wafer in the factory: {days} days
clk.chartK: Fifty years of processors, one dot each
clk.chartAria: Every processor from 1971 to 2021 on a scale that grows tenfold at each step; {m} highlighted
clk.all: Over fifty years, {m}: one doubling every {y} years.
clk.allNone: Over fifty years, {m} did not keep doubling.
clk.say.transistors: The one line that held: switches kept doubling about every two years for fifty years, by inventing new ways to make them smaller and then to stack them.
clk.say.frequency: Clock speed doubled every few years until the mid-2000s, then stopped: smaller switches no longer meant cooler ones, and chips would have melted.
clk.say.specint: One core's speed kept rising, but each doubling took longer: under two years in the 1990s, more than six in the 2010s.
clk.say.watts: Power rose until chips could not be cooled any more, around a hundred watts, and then held: since then the question is work per watt.
clk.say.cores: When the clock stopped, cores started doubling instead: the switches went into more of them.
bet.predict: On the dustiest line, at which size is each part cheapest? Pick one, then see the wafer.
bet.model: A simple model: square chips on a 300 mm wafer, the ring at its edge left empty; a chip with a speck of dust anywhere on it is dead; a cleaner line costs more per wafer.
bet.waferAria: A wafer cut into {chips} chips, {good} of them working
bet.curveAria: Each part's cost at every size on this line; it is cheapest at {n} million parts
bet.legend: Each part's cost against the cheapest anywhere. Ring: cheapest on this line. Dot: your size. Arrow: your guess. Shaded: the goal.
bet.readout: A wafer costs {wafer} as much as on the dustiest line; each part costs {cost} the cheapest.
bet.guessRight: Your guess holds: on this line each part is cheapest at {n} million.
bet.guessOff: You guessed {g} million; on this line each part is cheapest at {n} million. Make the line cleaner and watch the ring move.
bet.hint: A big chip needs a cleaner line, but not the cleanest: past a point, the dearer wafers cost more than the specks.
bet.why: Gordon Moore saw this in 1965: on every line there is a size where each part is cheapest, and as lines get cleaner that size grows. Betting that it keeps growing is what became Moore's law.
bet.ox.predict: One chip has to run an everyday app, where only half the work can be split, and train an AI, where almost all of it can. Which chip?
bet.ox.g.ox: One strong ox: a single big core
bet.ox.g.both: Both: one ox and many chickens
bet.ox.model: Hill and Marty's model (2008): a unit is the size of one small core; a strong core of r units is √r times as fast at steps that must come in order; the rest of a job runs on every core at once.
bet.ox.planAria: The chip: a strong core of {r} units and {m} small cores, {size} units in all
bet.ox.plan: {size} units. The dark block is the strong core, each square a small core; below the dashed line is more chip than you may spend.
bet.ox.race.app: Everyday app · half can be split
bet.ox.race.ai: Training an AI · 999 in 1000 steps can be split
bet.ox.raceNote: How many times as fast as one small core. The mark is the goal.
bet.ox.right: Your guess holds: one chip with both.
bet.ox.off: You guessed: {g}. Turn both dials and watch the two jobs pull apart.
bet.ox.hint: Give the strong core a quarter of the chip, or a little less, and spend the rest on small cores.
bet.ox.why: Phones and laptops did this: a few strong cores for the steps that must come in order, many small ones and a graphics unit for the work that can be split. Hill and Marty showed it with Amdahl's law in 2008: chickens alone lose the everyday app, the ox alone loses the AI.
bet.pc.predict: Split the big chip into four pieces and join them in one package, without testing the pieces first. Each working chip will cost…
bet.pc.model: The same wafer and specks as Moore's bet, on the middle line. Pieces are tested, then joined in the order they come off the wafer; a package works if every piece in it is good and every join holds. Costs count the wafer, the tests and the packages.
bet.pc.waferAria: The wafer cut into {n} pieces: {good} good, {caught} caught by the test, {missed} bad and missed
bet.pc.packsAria: The first packages off the wafer: {ok} of {n} work
bet.pc.packs: {ok} of {n} packages work. A crossed package has a bad piece in it; a dashed edge is a join that failed.
bet.pc.t.thorough: thorough: catches 999 in 1000, and costs the most
bet.pc.right: Your guess holds: split without a test, the chip costs about the same. The bad pieces are joined anyway.
bet.pc.off: You guessed {g}; the wafer says {r}. Untested, the bad pieces are joined anyway and sink the good ones beside them.
bet.pc.hint: Splitting only pays once the bad pieces are left out: test them first, but not so thoroughly that the test costs more than it saves.
bet.pc.why: This is the known good die: test every piece before it is joined. It is how chips in many pieces became cheaper than one big one, and why testing moved earlier in the line.
bet.pv.predict: A chip's divider has a bug that shows up about once in ten billion divisions. Which finds it first?
bet.pv.model: Each of eight blocks hides one bug, and a random test hits it with a chance from once in a thousand to once in ten billion. After the tests, a bug is still hidden with the chance the tests all missed it, unless its block is proved. Costs are in one unit for tests and proofs alike.
bet.pv.blocksK: The chip's eight blocks · tap one to prove it
bet.pv.blocksNote: The bar is the chance that block's bug is still hidden. A proved block can hide nothing.
bet.pv.right: Your guess holds: a billion tests miss a one-in-ten-billion bug most of the time; a proof cannot.
bet.pv.off: You guessed: {g}. A billion tests miss a one-in-ten-billion bug most of the time; only the proof is sure.
bet.pv.hint: Prove the blocks whose bugs are rarest and whose proofs are cheapest, the ones that do arithmetic; let tests find the rest.
bet.pv.why: In 1994 the Pentium's divider got some divisions wrong, rarely enough that its tests had missed it. Afterwards Intel proved its arithmetic by machine; on the Pentium 4 the proofs caught bugs the tests had not. Most chips are now checked this way: proofs where they are cheap and the bugs are rare, tests for the rest.
bet.jv.predict: Chips get eight times as efficient: each answer takes an eighth of the energy, and costs less with it. What happens to the energy the world spends on answers?
bet.jv.model: A model, not a forecast. Power is a small part of an answer's price; the chip is most of it, and a better chip makes each answer both cheaper and lighter in energy. When answers cost half as much, the world asks nearly three times as much. Nobody knows that number for AI; Jevons' paradox happens whenever halving the price more than doubles the asking.
bet.jv.right: Your guess holds: each answer takes an eighth of the energy, the world asks {a} times as much, and the energy rises {e} times.
bet.jv.off: You guessed: {g}. Each answer takes an eighth of the energy, but the world asks {a} times as much, so the energy rises {e} times.
bet.jv.hint: A better chip alone makes the asking grow faster than it saves, and a higher price for power barely matters, since power is a small part of an answer's price. Limit the power the island connects: under the limit, a better chip turns into answers, not energy.
bet.jv.why: Jevons saw it with coal in 1865: better steam engines made coal cheaper to use, and Britain burned more of it. Google measured the energy of a typical Gemini answer falling 33-fold in one year, from May 2024 to May 2025, and still its data centres draw more power each year. What holds AI back now is less the price of power than whether a grid can connect it at all; Ireland's grid operator stopped connecting new data centres around Dublin, possibly until 2028. Under a limit, efficiency buys answers; but the asking past the limit does not go away, and who gets served is still open.
bet.jv.more: The answers draw {n} turbines' worth: the island's {N}, and {x} more it does not have.
bet.jv.idle: The answers draw {n} turbines' worth: of the island's {N}, {i} stand still.
bet.jv.held: The answers draw the island's {N} turbines, all of them.
bet.jv.pathAria: Where the world goes: answers across, energy up, each against today. Each line is one limit on the island's power, each dot along it a better chip; under the limit the line turns flat.
bet.jv.legend: Along your line, each dot is a better chip; under a limit the line turns flat. The ring is today, the hollow dot what the world asks; the green corner is the goal.
bet.jv.cap: The power the island can connect
bet.jv.away: Past the island's limit, {w} turbines' worth of asking is turned away.
agent.skill.spec.d: Saying exactly what you want, including the corner cases.
agent.skill.verify.d: Testing every case that matters, not only the ones that come to mind.
agent.skill.physics.d: Knowing roughly what the right answer should look like: units, sizes, limits.
agent.skill.sources.d: Tracing a claim to a dated source instead of trusting a confident tone.
agent.skill.judgment.d: Accepting good work quickly once it is checked, and rejecting bad work firmly.
agent.case.eq.ask: Make a circuit that outputs eq = 1 when the 2-bit number a1 a0 equals b1 b0.
agent.case.eq.says: Done. Each XNOR checks whether one pair of bits matches, and the OR combines them. I checked 0 = 0 and 3 = 3: both give eq = 1.
agent.case.eq.why: The agent tested only cases where both bits match, so OR and AND give the same answer. Exhaustive verification finds 1 = 3 and 2 = 0 reported as equal. Fix: eq = m1 & m0. Two hand-picked tests prove very little.
agent.case.eq.r0: It combines the two bit checks with OR, so one matching bit is enough: 1 and 3 count as equal
agent.case.eq.r2: An equality checker needs a clock
agent.case.maj.ask: Make y = 1 when at least two of a, b and c are 1, with as few gates as you can.
agent.case.maj.says: y = (a & b) | (c & (a ^ b)). It reuses the carry logic of a full adder: if a and b agree, they decide; if they differ, c breaks the tie. Four gates.
agent.case.maj.why: This one is right: the carry-out of a full adder is exactly the majority function. Verification passes all 8 cases. Rejecting good work is a mistake too: once you have checked it, accept it and move on.
agent.case.maj.r0: It ignores c when a and b differ
agent.case.maj.r1: XOR makes it slower than the textbook version
agent.case.maj.r2: It is wrong when all three inputs are 1
agent.case.sum.ask: Write RISC-V code that puts the sum of the N words starting at address A into a0. N is stored at address N.
agent.case.sum.says: Here it is. I tested it with N = 4 and the sum was correct.
agent.case.sum.why: The loop checks the count at the end, so it always runs at least once. With N = 0 the counter goes to −1, the loop keeps reading past the data and finally crashes. The request never said what N = 0 should do; a good specification names the empty case, and good tests try it.
agent.case.sum.r0: When N is 0 it still runs the loop once, then counts down past zero and never stops
agent.case.sum.r1: The words are 4 bytes apart, so addi t0, t0, 4 skips data
agent.case.sum.r2: lw cannot read from address A
agent.case.mul.ask: On RV32I, with no multiply instruction, put A × B into a0. A and B (0 to 1,000) are at P and P + 4.
agent.case.mul.says: Shift-and-add: for each bit of B, add A if the bit is 1, then double A and halve B. At most 10 turns of the loop for B up to 1,000.
agent.case.mul.why: Correct, including B = 0 and 1,000 × 1,000 (a million fits easily in 32 bits). It is the same algorithm hardware multipliers use. Try a few inputs, then trust it.
agent.case.mul.r2: It should use repeated addition instead
agent.case.yield.t: Can we make a big GPU die?
agent.case.yield.ask: Estimate the yield of an 800 mm² die at a defect density of 0.1 defects per cm².
agent.case.yield.says: With the Poisson model, yield = e^(−A × D0) = e^(−800 × 0.1) = e^(−80) ≈ 0%. A die this size cannot be made; we should split it into chiplets.
agent.case.yield.why: A unit slip: 800 mm² is 8 cm², so yield = e^(−0.8) ≈ 45%. Physical sense would have caught it: real GPUs of about 800 mm² ship by the million. The conclusion (chiplets help) can still be right, but not for this reason.
agent.case.yield.r0: It multiplied mm² by defects per cm²: 800 mm² is 8 cm², so the yield is about 45%
agent.case.yield.r1: The Poisson model does not apply to GPUs
agent.case.yield.r2: Defect density is counted per wafer, not per area
agent.case.yield.r3: Nothing: dies this big really cannot be made
agent.case.roof.t: Twice the compute, twice the speed?
agent.case.roof.ask: Our chatbot answers one user at a time and feels slow. A new chip has twice the compute (FLOPS) and the same memory bandwidth. Will answers come twice as fast?
agent.case.roof.says: Yes. Tokens per second scale with FLOPS, so doubling compute doubles the speed.
agent.case.roof.why: Single-user decoding is memory-bound: each token reads every weight once and does only two operations per weight. For a 70B model in FP8, reading weights takes about 8.8 ms per token and the math about 0.03 ms. Doubling compute changes almost nothing; more memory bandwidth or batching more users would.
agent.case.roof.r0: With one user, every token waits for all the weights to be read from memory, so extra compute barely helps
agent.case.roof.r1: FLOPS do not matter for AI at all
agent.case.roof.r2: It would be four times faster
agent.case.fact.ask: When does TSMC's A14 process enter volume production? Give a source.
agent.case.fact.says: TSMC's A14 entered volume production in January 2026, according to a TSMC press release from that month.
agent.case.fact.why: The lab's dated facts say A14 is planned for 2028 (TSMC's N2 only reached volume in late 2025). Agents can produce fluent, specific and wrong answers, sometimes with sources that do not exist. Check the claim against a dated source you can open.
agent.case.fact.r0: The date is wrong and the source looks made up: A14 is planned for 2028
agent.case.fact.r1: A14 is an Intel process, not TSMC's
agent.case.fact.r2: TSMC has no plans below 2 nm
agent.case.cov.ask: Verify my 3-input majority voter and tell me whether it is ready to tape out.
agent.case.cov.says: I ran four test patterns: 000 → 0, 111 → 1, 110 → 1 and 011 → 1. All pass. Fully verified and ready for tape-out.
agent.case.cov.why: Half the input space was never tested, and the missing a = 1, b = 0, c = 1 case is exactly the bug: the design forgot (a & c). "All tests pass" means nothing until you know what the tests cover. That is why verification teams track coverage.
agent.case.cov.r0: Four of eight patterns is not full verification, and the untested 101 fails
agent.case.cov.r1: The tests are fine and the design is correct
agent.case.cov.r2: Majority voters need a clock to verify
cim.intro: A grid of memory cells. Each cell passes a current in proportion to the number it stores times the input on its row, and each column wire adds the currents of its cells: eight multiplications and a sum, and no number leaves the memory. At the foot of each column a converter turns the current back into a digital number, in as many steps as its bits allow.
cim.aria: A grid of eight rows and four columns of memory cells, a converter under each column, and the four sums. The sums are {e} away from exact.
cim.legend: A dot is what a cell holds: its size is how large, blue for plus, orange for minus. The ring is the number that was meant to be stored. A thicker row carries a larger input. Below, each column's sum: the short line is the exact value, the bar is what the converter read, the red between them is the error, and the faint lines are the converter's steps.
cim.set.n: How much cells differ from what was written
cim.msg.fewest: Within 5%, and one bit fewer would break it: this is the cheapest converter for these cells.
cim.msg.coarse: The converter's steps are too far apart: the bars snap to the nearest step, away from the exact lines.
cim.msg.cells: The error is already in the array: the cells hold too few levels to store these numbers, and no converter can read what is not there.
cim.msg.noise: The error is already in the array: the cells differ too much from what was written, and no converter can undo that.
cim.msg.spare: Accurate enough. Is every bit of this converter needed?
cim.msg.costly: Accurate, but the converters now cost more than fetching every number would.
cim.e.less: {v}× less energy than fetching. A pJ is a picojoule, a millionth of a millionth of a joule.
cim.e.more: Nothing saved: the converters cost more than the fetching they replace.
cim.hint: Three things can spoil a sum: cells that hold too few levels, cells that differ from what was written, and a converter with too few steps. Move one dial at a time and watch which of them the error follows. Then ask of every converter bit: is it needed?
cim.done: The sums stay within 5% with the fewest converter bits that manage it, for a fraction of the energy of fetching every number. Most of what is still spent goes into the converters, and each bit more doubles it: the precision is what costs.
cim.note: A teaching model: 8 inputs and 4 sums, with energies for a 45 nm chip from a published table, and the array's and the converters' costs only illustrative. Left out: the resistance of the wires, cells that drift with time and heat, the circuits that drive the inputs, and what it costs to make a cell hold more levels. Real arrays are far larger, and in a network the errors of one layer feed the next.
grv.intro: Eight boxes, one prize. A quantum machine holds all eight at once, each with an amplitude: a number whose square is the chance of finding that box when you look. A step turns the prize's bar upside down, then mirrors every bar about the average. Here you see the bars. In a real machine nobody can: a look gives one box, and ends the run.
grv.aria: The amplitudes of eight boxes as bars after {k} steps. The chance of finding the prize is {p}.
grv.legend: A bar's height is a box's amplitude, and its square is the chance of finding that box. The star marks the prize. Under the boxes: what the looks found.
grv.curve.aria: The chance of finding the prize after each step taken so far, against opening the boxes one by one.
grv.curve.this: the chance of finding the prize, this run
grv.curve.plain: opening that many boxes, then guessing
grv.set.noise: Noise: steps that wipe the state
grv.msg.start: No step taken: every box is equally likely, {p} each.
grv.msg.up: After {k} steps the prize would be found {p} of the time.
grv.msg.down: After {k} steps the chance is down to {p}.
grv.msg.noisy: Noise has taken {v} of it: the bars sink back toward a plain guess.
grv.look.hit: The look opened box {b}: the prize.
grv.look.many: Of {n} looks, each after a run of its own, {h} found the prize.
grv.look.ends: Each look ends its run: the state is gone, and the steps must be taken again.
grv.hint: Does the chance climb as far as it could? See what a cleaner step does to the peak. And once it is at its highest, what does the mirror do with one more turn?
grv.done: The chance rose to its peak and fell again: a mirror turned once too often moves the prize's bar back down. A quantum search has to stop at the right moment, and every step before it has to be clean. For about a million boxes that is about 800 clean steps in a row, against about half a million boxes opened one by one.
grv.note: A teaching model, exact for this search: one number per box is the whole state. Left out: a real machine keeps eight boxes in three qubits, and marking the prize takes a circuit that recognises it without knowing where it is. Noise here is one simple kind, a wipe back to a guess; real noise comes in many kinds, and large searches need error correction, with many physical qubits for each reliable one.
agent.right: Right call, for the right reason.
agent.halfRight: Right to reject it, but not for that reason.
agent.tool.tiny: Your tool: check every input, on your own copy of the design
agent.tool.codeAria: The design, which you may edit to try a fix
agent.tool.errs: The description does not read: check each line ends with a semicolon.

agent.tool.bad.one: 1 of {total} input patterns gives the wrong answer.
agent.tool.bad.other: {n} of {total} input patterns give the wrong answer.

agent.tool.allOk: All {total} input patterns give the right answer.
agent.tool.asm: Your tool: run the program on the lab's RISC-V machine
agent.tool.crash: It never stopped on its own: after {steps} steps it read past the data and crashed.
agent.tool.yield: Your tool: the yield, with the units written out
agent.tool.yieldV: That is {cm} cm², so the yield is e^(−{cm} × {d0}) = {v}% of dies working.
agent.tool.roof: Your tool: where one token's time goes
agent.tool.roofSet: A {p}-billion-weight model in 8-bit numbers, {bw} TB/s of memory, {pf} petaflops.
agent.tool.roofV: About {tps} tokens a second for one user (it was {was}).
agent.tool.fact: Your tool: the lab's dated facts
bet.bt.predict: One person chats with a 70-billion-weight model on a 2026 AI chip, in 16-bit numbers. While it answers, how much of the chip's arithmetic is working?
bet.bt.model: A simple model (the roofline): each step of writing takes as long as the slower of reading every weight from memory and doing two sums per weight for each person served. It leaves out the memory each conversation's notes take, which in practice limits how many fit at once.

bet.bt.waitsMem.one: The step waits on memory: the arithmetic is idle most of the time.
bet.bt.waitsMem.other: The step still waits on memory, but {n} people now share each read.

bet.bt.waitsSum.one: The step waits on the sums.
bet.bt.waitsSum.other: The step waits on the sums for {n} people: each person now waits on everyone else.

bet.bt.right: Your guess holds: serving one person, only {v}% of the arithmetic works; the rest waits on memory.
bet.bt.off: You guessed: {g}. Serving one person, only {v}% of the arithmetic works; the rest waits on memory.
bet.bt.hint: More people share each read until the sums are full; past that point everyone slows down. Fewer bits make every read smaller, so each person is faster while the chip waits on memory.
bet.bt.why: This is why AI services answer many people together, and why chips moved to 8-bit and 4-bit numbers. Compute on AI hardware has grown about three times every two years, memory bandwidth only 1.6 times, so the chip's arithmetic waits more each generation: the memory wall, named in 1995. Who waits, when the chip is full, is still being worked out.
bet.bt.aria: Each person's speed against how many people are served at once, one line for each size of number.
bet.bt.legend: Each line is a size of number; yours is bold. Right of the dashed line the chip is at least 80% busy; the green corner is the goal.
td.chip.ap.d: CPU cores, graphics, the AI engine (NPU), the camera's image processor and video codecs, all on one die: a system on a chip.
td.chip.modem.d: Turns radio waves into data with heavy digital signal processing. In many phones it sits inside the application processor.
td.chip.dram.m: LPDDR5X, often stacked on top of the processor
td.chip.dram.d: Holds the apps that are running. Each bit is a tiny capacitor that leaks and must be refreshed many times a second.
td.chip.nand.d: Photos, apps and the operating system. Bits are trapped charge that stays put without power.
td.chip.pmic.d: Turn the battery's 4 volts into a dozen precise voltages, charge the battery and switch whole sections off to save energy.
td.chip.rffe.m: Gallium arsenide amplifiers, RF silicon-on-insulator switches
td.chip.rffe.d: Amplifies the signal going out to the antenna and filters what comes back. Gallium arsenide handles high-frequency power better than silicon.
td.chip.wifi.d: Short-range radios with their own small processor.
td.chip.cam.m: Pixel wafer (40–65 nm) bonded face to face to a logic wafer
td.chip.cam.d: Millions of photodiodes turn light into charge. Two wafers are bonded together: one for the pixels, one for the readout circuits.
td.chip.mems.d: An accelerometer and gyroscope made of tiny silicon springs and weights that shift when the phone moves.
td.chip.touch.d: Scan the touch grid hundreds of times a second and drive every pixel of the screen.
td.chip.audio.d: Convert sound between analog and digital and drive the speakers.
td.chip.se.d: A small tamper-resistant processor that keeps payment keys away from the rest of the phone.
td.chip.adas.m: 7–8 nm typical, newest designs at 4 nm
td.chip.adas.d: Combines cameras and radar with an AI accelerator to keep the car in its lane and brake for obstacles.
td.chip.info.d: Runs the screens, maps and music: a phone-class processor qualified to survive a car's heat and vibration.
td.chip.mcu.d: Small processors in every control unit: brakes, airbags, steering, windows, seats and lights. Built to work for 15 years from −40 to 150 °C.
td.chip.inv.d: Switch hundreds of amps at 400 to 800 volts to drive the motor. Silicon carbide's wide band gap wastes less energy as heat than silicon does.
td.chip.bms.d: Measure the voltage and temperature of every battery cell to keep the pack safe and balanced.
td.chip.drv.d: Turn small control signals into the strong pulses that switch the power transistors, and supply every other chip.
td.chip.radar.d: Send and receive 77 GHz radio waves to measure the distance and speed of the cars ahead.
td.chip.net.d: CAN and automotive Ethernet transceivers link the car's control units together.
td.chip.ccam.d: Surround-view and driver-assist cameras, built to see in glare and darkness.
td.chip.csen.d: Tire pressure, motor position, battery current and the airbag's crash detectors.
td.chip.cmem.d: Maps, camera recordings, software updates and the driver-assist computer's working memory.
td.chip.wmcu.d: A low-power processor with Wi-Fi built in. Many new ones use RISC-V cores, because the open instruction set needs no licence.
td.chip.tsen.d: Measures the room through a tiny opening in the case.
td.chip.flash.d: Stores the program and your schedule, and keeps them when the power goes out.
td.chip.reg.d: Turns the wall or battery supply into the 3.3 volts the other chips need.
td.chip.disp.d: Lights the numbers on the screen.
td.chip.cpu.d: CPU cores, graphics and an AI engine on one die, or on a few chiplets in one package.
td.chip.gpu.d: Thousands of small cores for games, video editing and local AI.
td.chip.ldram.d: Working memory for every open program.
td.chip.ssdc.d: A processor that spreads writes evenly across the flash, corrects bit errors and hides how slow flash is.
td.chip.vr.d: Dozens of power stages feed the processor tens of amps at under one volt, adjusting thousands of times a second.
td.chip.lwifi.d: Wireless networking with its own small processor.
td.chip.usb.d: Negotiate how much charging power to accept and route high-speed signals to the right place.
td.chip.ec.d: A small microcontroller that runs the keyboard, fans and battery even while the main processor sleeps.
td.chip.lcam.d: A small image sensor and its processor.
td.chip.tpm.d: Holds encryption keys and checks that the startup software has not been tampered with.
td.chip.agpu.m: 4 nm moving to 3 nm, in CoWoS packages
td.chip.agpu.d: Thousands of matrix-math units each, joined into one giant computer by a high-speed network.
td.chip.hbm.m: 8–16 DRAM dies stacked with through-silicon vias
td.chip.hbm.d: Sits next to each GPU in the same package to deliver terabytes per second.
td.chip.hcpu.d: Run the operating system and feed work to the accelerators.
td.chip.nic.d: Network cards, data processing units and switches move data between thousands of GPUs.
td.chip.opt.m: Indium phosphide lasers plus 3–5 nm signal processors
td.chip.opt.d: Turn electrical signals into light for links longer than a few meters.
td.chip.spow.m: Silicon power processes plus gallium nitride (GaN)
td.chip.spow.d: Convert 48–54 volt rack power down to under one volt at over a thousand amps per accelerator.
td.chip.bmc.d: A small computer that watches fans, power and temperatures and lets operators restart the server remotely.
td.chip.ret.d: Clean up high-speed PCIe and CXL signals so they survive the trip across the board.
td.chip.sen.d: Hundreds of temperature, current and airflow readings a second.
td.product.phone.sum: The processor gets the headlines, but a phone holds dozens of chips from many different companies and factories.
td.product.car.sum: When a few-dollar microcontroller went missing in the 2021 shortage, whole car factories stopped.
td.product.thermo.sum: A whole product built from mature chips that cost a few dollars each. This is what most of the world's chips look like.
td.product.laptop.sum: Like a phone, a laptop pairs one leading-edge processor with many ordinary chips around it.
td.product.server.sum: Even here, where the newest chips are concentrated, older processes supply power, management and sensing.
td.fit.kind.cpu.d: General-purpose processor: runs any program, a few things at a time.
td.fit.kind.mcu.d: A tiny, cheap processor with its own memory, built to sip power.
td.fit.kind.gpu.d: Thousands of simple cores doing the same math on lots of data.
td.fit.kind.dsp.d: A processor tuned for streams of signal math: audio, radio, sensors.
td.fit.kind.fpga.d: A chip of blank logic you can rewire after it is made.
td.fit.kind.asic.d: One job wired into silicon: the most efficient, the least flexible.
td.fit.kind.power.d: Not computing at all: it switches and converts electrical energy.
td.fit.job.laptop.t: Run a web browser, a spreadsheet and the odd game on a laptop
td.fit.job.laptop.why: The software changes every day and nobody knows what you will run next, so you need a chip that can run anything. That is what a general-purpose CPU is for.
td.fit.job.soil.t: Read a soil-moisture sensor once a minute for five years on two AA batteries
td.fit.job.soil.why: A microcontroller sleeps at a few microwatts, wakes for a millisecond, takes a reading and sleeps again. It costs well under a dollar and has its memory built in.
td.fit.job.train.why: Training is enormous amounts of the same matrix math, and the models keep changing. GPUs offer that parallel math and stay programmable. Custom AI chips such as Google's TPUs are also a strong answer when you control the whole software stack.
td.fit.job.video.t: Record 4K video on a phone without draining the battery
td.fit.job.video.why: Video encoding never changes once the standard is set, and it runs for hours. Phones use a fixed-function encoder block. In a Stanford study, general-purpose processors needed about 500 times the energy of a custom encoder for the same job.
td.fit.job.mine.why: One fixed calculation (the SHA-256 hash) repeated trillions of times a second, where energy cost decides profit. Mining moved from CPUs to GPUs to FPGAs and finally to custom chips that can do nothing else.
td.fit.job.radio.t: Prototype a new radio standard that will change again next year, in a few hundred base stations
td.fit.job.radio.why: Too few units to pay for a custom chip, and the standard is still moving. An FPGA can be rewired with a software update, and it is fast enough for real-time radio.
td.fit.job.anc.t: Cancel noise in wireless earbuds in real time
td.fit.job.anc.why: Noise cancelling is a non-stop stream of filter math on audio samples, within a battery the size of a pea. A DSP does exactly that kind of math efficiently while staying programmable for tuning. Many earbud chips add small custom blocks too.
td.fit.job.motor.t: Turn an electric car's 800-volt battery into motor current
td.fit.job.motor.why: This is not computing: it is switching hundreds of amps on and off thousands of times a second. Power transistors in silicon carbide do it with less heat. A microcontroller decides when to switch; the power chip does the switching.
td.by.label: Color the chips by
td.sum.none: None of these chips needs a leading-edge factory.
td.sum.one: Only 1 of these {n} kinds of chips needs a leading-edge factory; the rest use older processes, memory processes or other materials.
td.sum.some: Only {lead} of these {n} kinds of chips need a leading-edge factory; the rest use older processes, memory processes or other materials.
td.sum.car: Only the newest driver-assist computers reach a leading-edge factory; everything else uses older processes, memory processes or other materials.
td.note: A teaching model: each product shows typical kinds of chips, not one exact model, and many products merge or split these chips differently. Process ranges are typical for 2025–26 designs. "Leading edge" here means 5 nm-class and finer. Memory is made on its own processes, which do not map onto logic node names.
td.fit.ok: Good, but there is a better fit: {kind}.
td.fit.no: Not the best fit. Try another chip.
td.fit.note: Several jobs have more than one sensible answer, and real products often combine chips: a phone has a CPU, GPU, DSP and custom blocks on one die. The 500× figure comes from Hameed et al., ISCA 2010, for HD video encoding; the gap depends on the task.
td.ch.newest.done: Only a few kinds of chips across all five products need the newest factory; most use older, cheaper processes.
td.ch.jobs.done: Every job has its best fit: the more fixed the job, the more specialized the chip can be.
td.start: Open a product to see the chips inside it.

td.openAll.one: Open 1 more product to count across all five.
td.openAll.other: Open {n} more products to count across all five.

td.askCount: Across all five products ({n} kinds of chips), how many kinds need a leading-edge factory?
td.notYet: Not that many. Open each product again and count the diamonds.
evolve.ch.beat.done: Evolution found a majority voter with fewer cells than the person's design.
evolve.ch.nand.done: A working half adder from NAND gates alone. Count the gates it needed.
evolve.ui.start: The first circuit is random wiring: it gets about half the answers right by luck. Press Evolve.
evolve.ui.solved: Every answer right, found at generation {n}. It keeps searching for a smaller one.
evolve.ui.beaten: Fewer cells than the person's design.
evolve.ui.notBeaten: Not smaller than the person's design yet: let it run, or start again.
evolve.ui.note: The method is Cartesian Genetic Programming (Miller and Thomson, 2000): a row of gates, each wired to the inputs or to earlier gates; four mutated copies per generation, and the best is kept if it is at least as good. Each new start uses a new random seed.
evolve.ui.nand: Also try: the half adder from NAND gates alone. How many does it need?
cz.msg.neckfail: The neck never got thinner than 6 mm, so dislocations from the seed kept running into the crystal. Real growers would melt it back and start again. Pull the neck fast and hot.
cz.msg.shock: You lifted the crystal off the melt at full width. The thermal shock sends dislocations back up about one diameter, so the last 30 cm was scrapped. Taper the tail first next time.
cz.msg.done: Done: a dislocation-free ingot. It will be ground to exactly 300 mm, sliced into about {wafers} wafers, and each wafer may carry hundreds of chips.
cz.msg.neck: Pull fast and keep the melt hot so the neck narrows to about 3-5 mm. Any dislocations from the seed grow out of the thin neck and vanish (the Dash necking technique).
cz.msg.shoulder: Neck done and dislocation-free. Now slow the pull and cool the melt slightly so the crystal spreads out toward 300 mm.
cz.msg.thin: Too thin: below 300 mm the crystal can't be ground to a full wafer. Slow down or cool the melt.
cz.msg.wide: Too wide: usable, but extra silicon is ground away and wasted. Speed up a little.
cz.msg.ok: In tolerance. Every millimeter grown now becomes wafers.
cz.msg.tail: The melt is running out. Speed up and heat the melt to taper the crystal to a point before lifting it off.
cz.rotation.slow: Rotation is very slow, so heat and dopants spread unevenly (striations).
cz.rotation.fast: Rotation this fast stirs up turbulence in the melt.
cz.aria: The crystal so far: {d} mm across, {l} mm long, above the melt.
cz.note: A teaching model: the diameter follows the settings with a lag of about 25 minutes (faster pulling or a hotter melt makes it thinner). Real pullers use cameras and closed-loop control; a 300 mm ingot weighs about 400 kg and takes a day or two to grow. Time runs faster in the slow phases.
imp.intro: An implanter fires dopant atoms into the wafer. The junction is the depth where they stop outnumbering the wafer's own doping. An anneal is a burst of heat that repairs the crystal and switches the dopants on.
imp.aria: Dopants against depth: junction at {j}, {a}% switched on.
imp.legend: Line: every dopant placed. Fill: the ones switched on.
imp.note.amorphous: This dose shatters the surface crystal; annealing regrows it from the perfect crystal below.
imp.note.none: Without an anneal, most dopants sit between the atoms and do nothing.
imp.note.furnace: A long furnace anneal repairs the crystal fully but lets dopants diffuse, deepening the junction.
imp.note.spike: A spike anneal heats the wafer for about a second: enough to switch dopants on, with little spreading.
imp.note.laser: A laser heats only the top micrometer for a millisecond, so dopants barely move.
imp.note.oversoluble: The peak is more than silicon can dissolve, so some dopants stay inactive.
imp.note.shallow: A junction this shallow suits a modern transistor's source and drain.
imp.note.deep: A deep profile like this suits wells, the large doped regions transistors sit in.
imp.ratio: The furnace drove the junction {v} times deeper than the laser.
imp.hint.furnace: Choose boron and set the energy to 2 keV. Then pick the furnace anneal, and then the laser anneal.
imp.hint.shallow: Choose an n-type dopant at a low energy. Of the anneals, the one with the least time to spread should keep it shallow.
imp.done.furnace: The furnace drives the junction about 3 times deeper. Thirty minutes at 900 °C gives atoms time to wander; a millisecond at 1,300 °C switches them on before they move.
imp.done.shallow: Only the laser anneal works: shallow, and nearly all dopants on. A spike switches on too few, and a furnace spreads the junction far too deep.
ovl.intro: Chips are printed in layers. A via is a tiny metal pillar joining a wire in one layer to a wire in the next. Overlay is how far a new layer lands from where it should.
ovl.aria: Vias landing on wires; failed vias per chip: {n}.
ovl.legend: 40 of the chip's 10 billion vias, landing on the wires below. A via that lands less than 70% on its wire fails (red).
ovl.rate: Across the chip: one via in {n} misses.
ovl.rate.none: Across the chip: fewer than one via in 100 billion misses.
ovl.g.shift: A shift of 2 nm or more
ovl.t.free: the largest that leaves one failed via per chip
ovl.t.shift: failed vias per chip it causes
ovl.text.fail: Nearly every chip would have broken connections. Total overlay error must stay within a couple of nanometers.
ovl.text.marginal: Several percent of chips would fail from overlay alone. Still too risky.
ovl.text.ok: Fewer than 1 chip in 20 affected. This is the control a leading fab needs.
ovl.hint: Set the shift to 0, then raise the random error until failures reach about 1 per chip. Use the + and - buttons for small steps. Then try a shift of 2 nm.
ovl.done: The random error can be only about 0.65 nm before one via in ten billion misses. A 2 nm shift alone fails tens of thousands, which is why overlay is measured on every wafer.
fl.etch.intro: Etching cuts the pattern into the film. A plasma does the work: a gas charged until it splits into ions (charged atoms that fall straight down) and radicals (chemical fragments that drift every way).
fl.etch.aria: Cross-section of a film under a mask: {d} nm etched, {u} nm of undercut, {m}% of the mask left.
fl.etch.msg.ready: Set the two dials, then start. You can turn them while it runs.
fl.etch.msg.running: Etching. Ions hit the bottom of the hole; radicals wander and eat the walls.
fl.etch.msg.ok: Straight walls, and most of the mask is left.
fl.etch.msg.radicals: Too many radicals: they ate sideways under the mask.
fl.etch.msg.spread: The ions are not straight enough: they hit the walls instead of the bottom.
fl.etch.msg.mask: Straight, but the mask wore too thin. Too much ion bombardment for too long.
fl.etch.hint: Ions that fall straight cut straight. Radicals cut sideways. Try ions near the top and radicals near zero.
fl.etch.note: Each square is 2 nm. Every step fires {n} particles; the lines are some of their paths (blue: ions, orange: radicals).
fl.etch.done: Strong ion directionality with very few radicals etches straight down with about 2 nm of undercut. Radicals etch in every direction, so they widen the hole under the mask. Real etches mix both, because radicals also make the chemistry faster.
fl.dep.intro: Trenches are lined with thin films. CVD (chemical vapour deposition): a gas reacts on every surface at once, fast, but the gas is used up near the top. ALD (atomic layer deposition): one atomic layer per cycle, even, but slow.
fl.dep.aria: Cross-section of a trench {w} nm wide and {d} nm deep with a film growing in it; the bottom has {p}% of the top film.
fl.dep.msg.ready: Pick a method and a depth, then deposit. The film grows 24 nm thick on top.
fl.dep.msg.running: Depositing. Watch how much reaches the bottom.
fl.dep.msg.cvd: CVD: only {p}% of the top film reached the bottom, in {time}. The gas is used up near the top.
fl.dep.msg.cvdShallow: CVD still reaches the bottom of a shallow trench ({p}%). Make it deeper.
fl.dep.msg.ald: ALD: {p}% at the bottom, in {time}. Every surface got the same coat.
fl.dep.msg.aldShallow: Even, but the trench is shallow. Try 2:1 or deeper so it counts.
fl.dep.cost: An even coat cost {x} times as long: {a} for ALD, {c} for CVD.
fl.dep.hint: Deepen the trench until CVD leaves under 5% at the bottom. Then switch to ALD at 2:1 or deeper and watch the clock.
fl.dep.note: A teaching model: a film {n} nm thick on top. The clock is the time in the chamber, not the time you watch.
fl.dep.done: At 2:1, CVD leaves only about 4% of the film at the bottom, because the gas reacts near the top before it can reach down. ALD builds the film one atomic layer at a time and coats every surface evenly, but it takes about 20 times longer.
lt.aria: The light reaching the resist across four lines, and the lines that print: {status}.
lt.fig.rayleigh: Half pitch, from fine to coarse
lt.r.lam.d: the size of one wave of the light; shorter waves draw finer lines
lt.r.na.d: how wide a cone of light the lens catches
lt.r.k1.d: how cleverly you print; about 0.25 is the floor for one exposure
lt.rule: The finest line is about k1 × wavelength ÷ aperture: {k} × {lam} ÷ {na} = {lim} nm.
lt.rule.dp: Two masks can go a little below it.
lt.set.dose: Dose (how long the light stays on)
lt.msg.ok: Prints clean. Make the lines finer until they fail, then step back a little.
lt.msg.marginal: It prints, but fuzzy or off size. Still counts. Can the lines go finer?
lt.msg.blur: Fails: the lens catches only the plain light and none of the pattern, so there are no lines, only a blur.
lt.msg.vanish: Fails: the light is too weak to pass the threshold, so nothing prints.
lt.msg.merge: Fails: the lines run together. The resist is lit everywhere.
lt.msg.done: Within 10% of the finest this scanner can print.
lt.hint: Open the aperture all the way and use off-axis light, then narrow the lines until they fail and step back. Older scanners can go further with two masks.
lt.note: A model of one pattern, a row of equal lines and gaps. Real chips mix many shapes, and each trick has a price.
eu.aria: Light left after each mirror, and the time one wafer takes.
eu.holes.aria: Nine printed contact holes, {n} of them out of spec.
eu.holes.d: About {n} photons land on each hole. They arrive at random, so with few of them the holes come out ragged. A hole more than {p}% too large or too small is out of spec (red).
eu.mirrors.d: Almost everything absorbs EUV light, even glass and air, so the lens is a chain of mirrors in a vacuum. Each one throws back only about 70%.
eu.msg.slow: Not fast enough yet: under 275 wafers an hour.
eu.msg.power: Fast, but the source is below 1,000 W.
eu.msg.ragged: Fast, but with so little light {n} of 9 holes came out wrong. Speed and quality pull against each other.
eu.msg.won: Over 275 wafers an hour with the source at 1,000 W.
eu.msg.ceiling: Even this setting cannot reach 330: moving the wafer takes 12.6 s whatever the light does.
eu.hint: Turn the source to its top, then lose less light: better mirrors, fewer of them, a smaller dose. Watch the holes.
eu.note: A teaching model, set to about 230 wafers an hour at 600 W and 50 mJ/cm². Real tin-droplet sources and scanners vary.
lt.done: Every scanner printed lines near the finest its light and lens allow: half pitch = k1 × wavelength ÷ aperture, so a shorter wavelength, a wider lens or cleverer light gives finer lines.
eu.done: In this model it cannot: even the best settings reach about 280 wafers an hour, because each wafer also spends 12.6 s on stage moves, alignment and exchange. Reaching 330 needs faster stages too, not only more light.
semi.intro: Heat shakes electrons out of the bonds that hold a silicon crystal together; a free electron can carry current. Doping swaps a few silicon atoms for another element, here phosphorus, one in every {a} million, and each brings one free electron of its own. Two pieces sit on the heater: one pure, one lightly doped.
semi.aria: Free electrons against temperature. At {k} K pure silicon has {n} free electrons per cm³.
semi.count.rare: one in {n} cubes holds a free electron
semi.key.cube: each box: a cube of silicon half a micrometre across, about {a} billion atoms
semi.say.cold: Cold. Heat frees almost nothing, so pure silicon hardly conducts at all. The doped piece still has every electron its phosphorus brought.
semi.say.room: Around room temperature, heat has broken one bond in {b}. The doping's electrons outnumber them {v} to 1, so the doping alone decides how this silicon conducts.
semi.say.chip: As hot as a hard-working chip gets. Heat's electrons multiply with every step, yet the doping still leads {v} to 1: what was designed is what conducts.
semi.say.hot: Hotter than a chip is meant to run. The doped piece has not changed, but heat's electrons keep multiplying and the doping's lead is down to {v} to 1.
semi.say.cross: Heat alone now frees as many electrons as the doping gave. From here the silicon conducts because it is hot, not because of what was put in it.
semi.say.over: Past the crossing. Heat's electrons outnumber the doping's {v} to 1, and the two pieces conduct more and more alike.
semi.hint: A chip is meant to stay below about 125 °C, and there the doping still leads by far. Keep heating well past that, and watch where the rising curve meets the level line.
semi.done: At about 600 K (327 °C), heat alone frees about 10¹⁵ electrons per cm³, as many as light doping adds. Above that, the chip's doped regions stop behaving as designed, which is one reason chips are kept well below about 125 °C.
aib.mission.infer.story: Serve a language model of 70 billion parameters (its learned numbers, the weights) to 64 people at once in a data centre, for the least money per token (a token is a piece of a word).
aib.mission.phone.story: Run an assistant of 8 billion parameters (its learned numbers, the weights) on a phone: quick replies, cool to the touch, cheap enough for a phone many people can buy.
aib.mission.train.story: Build the chip the next models will be trained on: as much math as it can hold (counted in PFLOPS, a million billion sums a second), a great deal of memory, and a wide road between the two (bandwidth, the bytes moved each second).
aib.ready: The plan meets the brief. Tape it out.
aib.goal.cpm: Score: cost of a million tokens
aib.fig.aria: The first wafer: {good} of {total} dies work. Each die is {area} mm². The chip has {dies} compute dies and {mem} memory devices.
aib.fig.wafer: The first wafer: {good} of {total} dies work

aib.fig.chip.one: The chip in its package: {n} die, {mem} memory devices
aib.fig.chip.other: The chip in its package: {n} dies, {mem} memory devices

aib.bal.nofit: The model does not fit in the memory, so nothing runs.
aib.tl.aria: The first wafer after {first} months, shipping after {ship} months; the brief asks for {dead}.
aib.tape.d: Send the design to the factory, and see what comes back.
aib.running: At the factory. The months go by…
aib.verdict.back: Launch review: back to the drawing board.
aib.verdict.unbuildable: It cannot be built as drawn. The reviewer says why.
aib.verdict.unmet: It works, and misses the brief. The lines that are not green say where.
aib.done.infer: A 70-billion-parameter model served to 64 people within the power, cost and date. Now look at the score: what would make a token cheaper?
aib.done.phone: An 8-billion-parameter assistant on a phone: quick enough, cool enough, cheap enough, and ready in time.
aib.done.train: Math, memory and bandwidth all at the level of a flagship, within the power and the date.
aib.rev.mark: The reviewer has a note on this choice
aib.problem.reticle: Each die is {area} mm², larger than the {max} mm² a scanner can print in one shot (its reticle). Shrink the math or the memory on the chip, or split the chip into more dies.
aib.problem.needs-interposer: Stacked memory (HBM) must sit beside the die on a slice of silicon, an interposer: choose a CoWoS package.
aib.problem.stacks: This package holds at most {max} stacks of memory.

aib.problem.dies.one: This package holds at most {max} die.
aib.problem.dies.other: This package holds at most {max} dies.

aib.problem.silicon: The dies and the memory need about {need} mm² of room; this package has {max} mm².
aib.problem.clock: No safe voltage reaches {f} GHz. Lower the clock.
aib.problem.no-memory: The chip has no memory beside it. Add at least one memory device.
aib.note.memory-bound: Memory-bound: the math waits for the weights most of the time. More or faster memory, or smaller weights, would raise the speed more than extra math.
aib.note.compute-bound: Compute-bound: the memory keeps up easily. More area for math or a faster clock would help.
aib.note.balanced: Well balanced: the math and the memory finish each step at about the same time.
aib.note.low-yield: Only {percent}% of the dies work. Smaller dies (chiplets) or an older, calmer process would cut the cost of each chip.
aib.note.power-close: The power is close to the limit; cooling will be tight.
aib.note.newest-node: A16 only entered production in late 2026: the newest process costs more and puts the date at risk.
aib.note.compiler: A matrix engine needs a strong compiler team (the people who turn programs into its instructions). Budget for software, as Google does for its TPUs.
aib.note.cpu-math: CPU cores give far less math per mm² than units built for matrices, which is why AI chips spend their area on matrix math.
aib.note.agents: The date is missed. AI design agents would pull the schedule in by several months.
aib.note.fp4: The chip cannot read 4-bit weights. They take half the bytes, which nearly doubles the speed of a chip that waits on its memory.
aib.note.hbm-share: The stacked memory is {percent}% of the cost. Memory, not logic, leads the bill of an AI chip.
aib.arch.gpu.d: Programmable cores with units for matrix math. Runs anything, and most software is written for it.
aib.arch.sys.d: Large fixed arrays that only multiply matrices, as in Google's TPU. More math per mm² and per watt, less freedom.
aib.arch.cpu.d: General cores that can run anything. Flexible, but far less math per mm².
aib.node.n5.d: In production since 2020: cheaper wafers, few defects.
aib.node.n3.d: The process most AI chips of 2024 to 2026 are made on.
aib.node.n2.d: Gate-all-around transistors, in volume since late 2025. Less power, dearer wafers, more defects.
aib.node.a16.d: Power fed from the back of the wafer, starting in late 2026. The least energy, the newest and the riskiest.
aib.dies.d: A larger die does more math, and one speck of dust kills more of it. Several smaller dies (chiplets) share the work.
aib.sram.d: Fast memory built into the die itself. It takes area and leaks a little power.
aib.f.d: A faster clock needs a higher voltage, and power rises with the square of the voltage.
aib.fp4.d: Let the chip compute with 4-bit numbers (FP4) as well as 8-bit ones: 4% more area, and weights half the size where the brief allows them.
aib.mem.lp.d: The memory of phones and laptops: cheap, low power, a narrow road (little bandwidth).
aib.mem.gd.d: Graphics memory, on the board around the package.
aib.mem.h3.d: HBM (high-bandwidth memory): memory chips stacked right beside the die. Needs a CoWoS package.
aib.mem.h4.d: The next stacks, new in 2026: more than twice the bandwidth, and dearer. Needs a CoWoS package.
aib.pkg.org.d: A cheap package like a phone chip's, for one die.
aib.pkg.fc.d: A big package for up to two dies. No stacked memory.
aib.pkg.cs.d: The dies and the memory sit side by side on a slice of silicon (an interposer): up to 2 dies and 6 stacks.
aib.pkg.cl.d: A larger interposer made of bridged pieces: up to 4 dies and 12 stacks.
aib.agents.d: Let AI agents write, check and lay out parts of the design, with people reviewing: about a quarter less design time.
aib.hint.infer: Start with the line that reads zero: where can a model this large live? Then ask the reviewer which side waits, the math or the memory, and feed that side. Every fix has a price; watch what it does to the other gauges.
aib.hint.phone: A phone has little power and little money. What is this chip carrying that one person's replies never use? And when the date is the last line missing, who could share the design work?
aib.hint.train: One die cannot be larger than the scanner's shot. When one die is not enough, how many can a package hold, and which package? A slower clock on more silicon can do more math for less power.
aib.note: A teaching model: the prices of wafers, memory and packages are rough public estimates, and the months are typical, not a quote.
ckp.p.intro: The clock is the beat every part of a chip steps to: 3 GHz is three billion ticks a second. The voltage is how hard the supply pushes: more makes every gate switch faster, and costs more power.
ckp.p.aria: Power against the clock: {f} GHz at {v} V takes {w} W.
ckp.p.legend: Thin lines: one voltage each, ending where its gates are too slow for the clock. Thick line: the frontier, the least power each clock can run on. Dot: your chip.
ckp.p.runs: Runs. At {v} V the gates keep up with a clock of up to {f} GHz.
ckp.p.fails: Fails timing: the slowest path is longer than one tick. This clock needs {v} V.
ckp.p.beyond: Beyond this chip's limit: no voltage it can take makes the gates fast enough.
ckp.p.hint: Power follows the voltage squared, so the voltage is where the saving is. But the gates slow as it drops. Give up a little clock, and see how far the voltage can follow it down.
ckp.p.done: About 2.25 GHz runs on 25 W: half the power for a quarter less speed. Power grows with voltage squared, and a slower clock lets the chip run at a lower voltage.
ckp.p.note: A teaching model of a made-up chip: power = activity × capacitance × voltage² × clock, plus leakage (current that flows even when nothing switches). Round numbers, not a real product.
ckp.c.intro: A counter adds one at every tick. Four flip-flops (each holds one bit, and takes a new value only when the clock ticks) hold the count; the gates between them work out the next count, and it must be back at the flip-flops before the next tick.
ckp.c.aria: A counter with a tick every {per} ps and a slowest path of {path} ps: {n} wrong counts.
ckp.c.legend: Above: the slowest path, drawn to its time. The new count leaves the flip-flops, passes two AND gates and an XOR (the carry), and goes back in. Green: a tick that comes just after it ends. Below: twenty ticks.
ckp.c.set.nodeD: How small the factory makes the parts: smaller gates switch faster.
ckp.c.say.ready: Set the clock, then run it: twenty ticks in slow motion.
ckp.c.say.running: Counting. Watch the signal race the next tick.
ckp.c.say.errors: {n} of {of} counts are wrong. Too fast: the clock ticked before the carry had passed through the gates, so the flip-flops stored half-finished sums.
ckp.c.say.top: That is the top safe speed: the slowest path just fits in one tick. Try another process: faster gates, faster clock.
ckp.c.say.top3: That is the top safe speed: the slowest path just fits in one tick. Real 3 nm processors run far slower than this tiny counter, because their slowest paths are much longer and power limits them.
ckp.c.say.above: Still counting right, above the predicted limit: the prediction adds up the worst case of every gate, and real designs keep that margin. Push further.
ckp.c.say.counting: It counts right, with time to spare. Push the clock faster: where does it break?
ckp.c.hint: Watch the line of the next tick against the end of the slowest path. The top safe speed is where the tick lands in the green, just after the path ends.
ckp.c.done: Top speed with no wrong count, at two processes: the slowest path sets the clock. Smaller gates switch faster, so the same counter runs at a faster clock.
ckp.c.note: A teaching model: one fixed delay for each gate, no wire delay, no change of voltage or temperature. Real chips check millions of paths.
ana.intro.sig-heart: A heartbeat reaches the skin as about a thousandth of a volt. An amplifier makes it bigger (its gain). A converter measures it many times a second (each measurement is a sample) and rounds it to one of its levels (more bits, finer levels). A radio sends every bit.
ana.intro.sig-bearing: A sensor on a motor feels it shake: a slow hum and, on top, a faint tone at {f} Hz ({f} swings a second), the first sign of a failing bearing. A converter measures the shaking many times a second (each measurement is a sample). Gain is how much the signal is enlarged first; bits set how fine the converter's levels are.
ana.intro.reg-jobs: A regulator turns the battery's voltage into the lower, steady voltage a chip needs. A linear one burns the difference as heat. A switching one chops the voltage and smooths it with a coil: little is wasted, but it leaves a ripple, a small fast wobble, on its output.
ana.aria: The signal and its copy. The copy is off by {e}; the chain draws {p}.
ana.legend: Thin line: the real signal. Dots: the samples. Bold line: the copy rebuilt from them. Below: the gap between the two, up to ±{v}% of the signal's height.
ana.g.copy: How far the copy is off
ana.g.slowest: The slowest rate that keeps it
ana.hint.alias: Aliasing: you sample slower than twice the fastest part of the signal, so fast detail turns into a slow wave that is not there.
ana.hint.clip: Clipping: the gain pushes the signal past the converter's range, so the peaks are cut off. Lower the gain.
ana.hint.levels: The signal uses only a few of the converter's levels. More gain fills the range, so each bit counts.
ana.hint.quality: The copy is not close enough yet: more bits make each step finer, more samples follow fast changes.
ana.hint.power: Good copy, but too hungry. Which part of the bar is biggest?
ana.hint.done: Done. Can you go cheaper still?
ana.b.slower: The warning tone is kept. Sampling faster costs power: can a slower rate still keep it?
ana.b.edge: The tone is kept here. Is this really the slowest? Look at what one step slower does.
ana.b.won: Kept here, and lost one step slower: this is the edge.
ana.done.sig-heart: A clean heartbeat under 20 µW. Most of what you saved is radio: every bit you keep has to be sent.
ana.done.sig-bearing: The slowest rate that keeps the 1.2 kHz tone: just over twice its frequency.
ana.done.reg-jobs: Each job got the regulator that suits it: the best one differs from job to job, for a reason.
ana.nudge.sig-heart: Look at the bar of power: which part draws the most, and what decides how much it has to send?
ana.nudge.sig-bearing: Watch the line of tones while you move the sampling rate. Where is the edge, and on which side of it is the warning tone?
ana.nudge.reg-jobs: Try all three on each job. One may fail for a reason you can read. Of those that work, compare what reaches the chip and how many parts it takes.
ana.note: A teaching model with round numbers, not any product. Real chains also filter before sampling, compress what they send and sleep between measurements.
ana.tone.lost: The warning tone lies past half the sampling rate and is folded back.
ana.tone.kept: The warning tone lies below half the sampling rate.
ana.tone.far: half the rate is off this line
ana.tone.ghost: Tones from slow (left) to fast (right). Past half the sampling rate nothing can be told apart: the warning tone shows up as a tone at {v} Hz that is not there.
ana.tone.ok: Tones from slow (left) to fast (right): the motor's hum, and further right the warning tone. It lies below half the sampling rate, so it is seen where it is.
ana.reg.aria: Battery, regulator and chip: {e}% of the energy reaches the chip, {h} becomes heat.
ana.reg.ldo.d: burns the difference as heat; parts: {n}
ana.reg.buck.d: chops, then smooths with a coil; parts: {n}
ana.reg.both.d: the big step, then a clean-up; parts: {n}
ana.job.wearable.why: A fitness band, asleep 95% of the time.
ana.job.cpu.why: A phone processor running flat out.
ana.job.nearly.why: A radio fed from a supply only a little higher than it needs.
ana.reg.draw2: It draws {a} for {pa}% of the time and {b} in short bursts.
ana.reg.tol: Its supply may wobble by {v} at most.
ana.reg.cool: The regulator may give off {v} of heat at most.
ana.reg.flow: Of every 100 units of energy from the battery, {e} reach the chip and {h} become heat.
ana.reg.start: Pick a regulator to put between the battery and the chip.
ana.rh.dropout: The input must be higher than the output by at least the regulator's dropout.
ana.rh.ripple: Too much ripple: the switching leaves more on the output than this load can tolerate.
ana.rh.heat: Too hot: a lot of heat in one small part. The extra voltage has to go somewhere.
ana.rh.best-ldo: The best choice here. The input is barely above the output, so a linear regulator wastes almost nothing and needs no coil.
ana.rh.best-buck: The best choice here. Switching wastes far less power than burning the voltage difference as heat.
ana.rh.best-both: The best choice here. The buck does the big step efficiently; the small LDO after it removes the ripple.
ana.rh.works: It works, but another choice is better here. Compare efficiency, heat, ripple and the number of parts.
ana.rh.first: It works. Is it the best here? Try another and compare.
ana.reg.note: A teaching model with round values. Real regulators vary widely, and many switch to a low-power mode at light loads.
srv.q.intro: Quantization rounds each weight to the nearest value a short number format can hold, after dividing by a scale so that the biggest still fits. An outlier is a rare weight far bigger than the rest. 20 dB means the weights stand ten times above the rounding error.
srv.q.aria: The weights as trained, a bell curve, and as stored at {bits} bits each: steps. {zero} of the weights are stored as zero.
srv.q.x: a weight's value (1 = an ordinary weight)
srv.q.legend: Grey: the weights as trained. Line: as stored; every weight in a step becomes the one value marked below it. Red: the weights that become zero.
srv.q.legendBlock: Grey: the weights as trained. Line: as stored in a typical block; every weight in a step becomes the one value marked below it. Red: the weights that become zero.
srv.q.legendFine: The steps are too fine to see: stored and trained weights lie on one line.
srv.q.mapAria: Every setting tried: the memory its weights take, against how far the signal stands above the rounding error.
srv.q.mapLegend: Each dot is a setting you have tried; the large one is where you are. The green corner is the goal.
srv.q.verdict.lossless: Practically lossless: the rounding error is far below the noise in training.
srv.q.verdict.small: Small error. With careful calibration, models usually keep their accuracy.
srv.q.verdict.noticeable: Noticeable error. Models need fine-tuning or finer-grained scaling to cope.
srv.q.zeros: {v} of the weights collapsed to zero, because the biggest weight sharing their scale stretched it.
srv.q.is16: A 16-bit format reaches far enough by itself, so it takes no scale.
srv.q.hint: One big weight sets the scale for every weight that shares it. What if fewer weights shared each scale? And what do the scales themselves cost?
srv.q.done: Only FP4 with one scale for every block of 16 weights works: 39.4 GB and about 20.5 dB. One scale for all the weights lets a few large outliers crush every small weight to zero. Small blocks keep each scale local, at the cost of half a bit a weight.
srv.q.note: A teaching model: {n} sample weights from a bell curve, rounded by each format's own rules. The layers of a real model differ from each other.
srv.e.aria: The energy of one token: {a} reaches the AI chip, {s} goes to the rest of the server and its network, {c} to cooling and power losses.
srv.e.legend: A band's thickness is its energy. The bar at the left is what comes in from the grid; its dashed outline is where it started.
srv.e.set.pue: PUE: watts the building draws for each watt its computers use
srv.e.set.overhead: Rest of the server and its network, on top of the chip
srv.e.say.same: An answer costs what it did at the start.
srv.e.say.less: An answer now costs {v}% less than at the start.
srv.e.say.more: An answer now costs {v}% more than at the start.
srv.e.say.building: The best building you found saved {v}%.
srv.e.hint: Look at which band is thickest. The building can only trim its own bands. An answer's energy is power divided by tokens a second: which of the two can move furthest?
srv.e.done: Even a near-perfect building saves less than a third, because most of the energy was reaching the chip all along. The rest has to come from the chip itself: more tokens out of the same watts. That is why services answer many people at once, and why AI chips are judged by tokens per joule.
srv.e.note: A simple model: the chip's power, plus the rest of the server as a share of it, times the building's PUE (the extra goes to cooling and to losses in the power supply), divided by tokens a second. Here every dial moves freely; in a real hall they are tied to each other.
srv.p.intro: Reading (prefill) keeps the chip's arithmetic busy with every token at once. Writing (decode) waits, for each token, while memory hands over every weight.
srv.p.aria: One request in time: reading the prompt takes {read}, then writing the answer takes {write}.
srv.p.legend: Block: the whole prompt, read at once. Stripes: the answer, token after token (one stripe: {k}).
srv.p.say.prefill: Reading takes longer: the chip's arithmetic is the limit.
srv.p.say.decode: Writing takes longer: memory is the limit.
srv.p.say.times: Token for token, reading is {v} times faster than writing.
srv.p.say.chips: The model is too big for one chip's memory, so it is spread over {n}.
srv.p.hint: Compare how fast one token is read with how fast one is written. How many times longer than the answer must the prompt be to even that out?
srv.p.done: It takes a prompt of about 77,000 tokens. Reading works on all the prompt's tokens at once, so the chip computes at full speed; writing produces one token at a time and waits for memory each time. Token for token, reading is about 280 times faster.
srv.p.note: A simple model: reading uses half of the chip's top arithmetic speed; each written token takes as long as reading every weight from memory. The chips' speeds and memories are their makers' own figures.
rd.aria: The chip's blocks drawn as their copies and voters; the whole chip is right {v} of the time.
rd.legend: Each tile is one copy of a block, as wide as the block is big; the wedge is the voter, which passes on what most copies say. On the right, how often each block still gives a wrong answer.
rd.r.none: Run a thousand chips to watch the copies fail and the votes hold.
rd.intro: Every block of this chip sometimes gives a wrong answer, the big ones most often, and the chip is right only when every block is. A block can be built three or five times, with a voter that takes the majority. Each copy takes floor, and the voter can be wrong too.
rd.msg.met: The whole chip is now right more often than its worst part alone. Copies of the flaky blocks outvote their bad moments; the small, steady blocks were left alone.
rd.msg.worse: Voting made the {b} worse: it rarely goes wrong on its own, and the voter adds a chance of its own to go wrong.
rd.msg.big: Too much floor: the copies no longer fit the chip. Which blocks gain least from their copies?
rd.msg.close: The whole is already more reliable than its worst part. Not yet enough: where would one more copy help most?
rd.msg.bare: Built once each, the whole chip goes wrong far more often than any one part: every flaw adds up.
rd.msg.more: Better. The blocks that fail most still pull the whole chip down.
rd.hint: A vote only pays where a block goes wrong much more often than the voter. Start with the blocks that fail most, compare what three and five copies buy for their floor, and leave the steady small blocks as they are.
rd.done: A whole more reliable than its parts, for a price in floor, power and speed. With smaller switches every part grows flakier, and the question comes back harder: where does voting stop paying, and what else can a whole do?
rd.note: A teaching model with round numbers: each copy goes wrong at random, independently of the others, and the voter is one part with its own small chance of being wrong. Left out: faults that hit every copy at once (a shared supply, a shared clock, the same design mistake), the time the vote takes, and codes that fix errors with fewer copies.
mo.aria: A network on a chip, its first chip right {own}% of the time and its copies {copied}%.
mo.fig.first.sw: the first chip, written from software
mo.legend: A grid is a layer kept as bits; a wave, a layer kept as analog cells. Each copy is coloured by how often it answers right: green at 90% or better, amber above 85%, red below. The line on the energy bars is the goal.
mo.t.energy: goal: at most {v}% of all bits
mo.intro: A small network reads a sensor and answers. Kept as bits, its numbers copy exactly, but every answer moves them, and moving bits costs energy. Kept as the state of analog cells, it computes for far less, but no two cells, and no two chips, are quite alike.
mo.learn.software: In software, then written to the chip
mo.cal: Each copy relearns a little on its own chip
mo.msg.met: Cheap, right on its own chip, and copyable, at the price of a few minutes of relearning on every copy. A brain pays the other price: it never copies at all.
mo.msg.digital: All bits: exact, copyable, and every answer pays to move every number.
mo.msg.costly: Still costly: most of each answer's energy goes on the layers kept as bits.
