mo.msg.brain: Like a brain: it learned around its own chip's quirks and works well there, but on any other chip those quirks are wrong. What it knows dies with the chip.
mo.msg.blind: Learned in software, it copies faithfully, but it never saw this chip's quirks, so every chip, the first too, answers worse.
mo.msg.more: Close. One of the three still falls short.
mo.hint: Try the three ways of learning at a high analog share, and watch the copies change colour. Learning on the chip fits one chip; learning in software fits none exactly. What if each copy fits itself?
mo.done: Copyable and cheap, but only by relearning on every copy, and the more is analog, the longer that takes. Is that a machine that copies its mind, or one that grows a new one each time from a shared start?
mo.note: A teaching model with round numbers, not measurements: analog layers about twelve times cheaper per answer than bits, every analog cell off by about 10%, and accuracy falling with the square of the noise. Left out: cells that drift with time and heat, the cost of the converters at each layer's edge, and networks trained to tolerate noise.
xray.type.dram.clue: Huge, extremely dense arrays split by thin strips: almost the whole die is memory.
xray.type.pixels.clue: A vast field of tiny coloured squares: one light-sensitive pixel each, under red, green and blue filters.
xray.type.adc.clue: A long, thin strip of identical columns along the pixel array: one converter for each column of pixels.
xr.why.mcu: Most of the area is memory (flash for the program, SRAM to work in) and analog circuits that talk to the outside world. The processor itself is a speck.
xr.why.phone: A block for each job: big and little processor cores, graphics, an AI engine, image and video engines, and memory links along the edge.
xr.why.gpu: A sea of identical cores, with a band of cache across the middle and links to the stacked memory down both sides.
xr.why.dram: Almost the whole die is memory arrays, with a thin strip of control logic and a row of pads down the middle.
xr.why.camera: Most of the area is the pixel array, with a row of converters above and below it, one for each column of pixels.
xr.ask: What kind of chip is this?
xr.wiring: That is wiring and spacing between the blocks.
xr.g.found: Every block found on one die
xr.cleared: Dies read to the last block: {n}
xr.aria: A photo of a chip's die, its blocks drawn with the textures they have under a microscope.
xr.done: You can read a die: memory as a regular grid, logic as fine noise, copies of one tile, hand-drawn shapes, and the share of area that tells what a chip is for. A die photo is one way to check a chip; what is hidden below the top layer, or in its design, is the harder part.
er.intro: From the job the chip does down to its package, each row is a level of the chip: the wrong values born there, what that level's protection stops, and the protection itself. What gets past every level leaves at the top as silent wrong answers, counted in every billion answers.
er.placed.phone: A 2-second answer from an assistant on the phone, with 64 megabits of memory in use.
er.placed.car: One millisecond step of a brake controller, through fifteen hot years. The car standard at its highest level asks for fewer than 10 failures in a billion hours.
er.placed.datacentre: A large language model writing an answer in a hall of machines, where rare for one machine is daily for the hall.
er.placed.space: One second of a satellite's computer, built like a car's, in low orbit, where particles flip bits thousands of times more often.
er.inHours: in a billion hours of work
er.bornT: {v} wrong values born here in a billion answers
er.stopT: {v} stopped here in a billion answers
er.nohall: Only a hall of machines can take some out to test them.
er.msg.met: Right enough, within what this place allows. About {caught} answers in a billion are still caught: refused or redone, never wrong.
er.msg.costly: Being right costs more area or energy than this place allows. Which protection buys least here?
er.msg.worst: Most of the silent answers left come from {src}. Which level can see them?
er.all: Phone, car and data centre cleared: the same faults, met at different levels by each.
er.hint: Look at where the silent answers are born, and protect at a level that can see them: codes on memory for flipped bits, a margin for late signals, copies or self-test for copies born broken. A car must pay for a second copy of its logic; a data centre cannot, but it can check its arithmetic and hunt bad machines in the fleet.
er.done: Silent errors can be made rare, never impossible, and each power of ten costs more. When no one can check every answer, what is the trust in a machine resting on?
er.note: The puzzle's engine (src/engines/errors.js): the rates of particles, broken copies and stopping machines are from sources, the rest are choices said to be in the code. It is fair enough to compare plans and never wrong in direction, not a reliability simulator.
rv.intro: The core of the community's computer runs RISC-V. Each puzzle puts its numbers in a1 and a2; your program leaves the answer in a0. Run checks it on every case, then Play shows the core working through the first one.
rv.aria: The core at work: the program, the program counter, the decoder showing {op}, the arithmetic unit and the registers.
rv.err.label: there is no label called {n}.
rv.err.unknown: {n} is not an instruction this core knows.
rv.err.range: {n} is too big for this instruction.
rv.err.operands: this instruction needs a different number of operands.
rv.err.memop: write a memory address as offset(register), for example 0(t0).
rv.err.mem: the program reached outside the memory.
rv.err.needM: {n} needs a multiplier, and this core has none.
rv.err.needMAC: {n} needs the AI unit, and this core has none.
rv.err.needDOT4: {n} needs the AI unit's four-way multiplier, which this core does not have.
rv.forbid: This puzzle is to be solved without {op}.
rv.slow: Right, but it takes {v} cycles. There is a way with far fewer.
rv.p.sum.d: a0 = 1 + 2 + … + a1. This one already works: run it and watch the loop go round.
rv.p.max.d: a0 = the larger of a1 and a2. A branch skips a line when a comparison is true.
rv.p.mul.d: a0 = a1 × a2. This core has no multiplier: build one from additions.
rv.p.fib.d: a0 = the a1-th number of 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 …, each the sum of the two before it.
rv.p.fast.d: a0 = 1 + 2 + … + a1 again, now with a multiplier, in 12 cycles or fewer even for a1 = 1000.
rv.ok.sum: Solved. Every turn of the loop is three instructions; adding to 100 takes about 300 steps.
rv.ok.max: Solved. A compare and a jump: that is all an "if" is, inside a processor.
rv.ok.mul: Solved, with additions only. Early processors multiplied this way; a multiplier in hardware does it in one step, for the price of its area.
rv.ok.fib: Solved. Two registers carry the last two numbers, and a third makes the next.
rv.ok.fast: Solved: the same answer in a handful of cycles, by an idea instead of a loop. Better hardware or a better idea: which do you reach for first?
rv.hint.sum: Press Run, then Play. Watch t2 count up and a0 grow, and the branch jump back to the top of the loop.
rv.hint.max: Copy a1 into a0 with mv. Then compare: if a1 is already at least a2 (bge), jump past the line that copies a2 into a0.
rv.hint.mul: Add a1 to a0 again and again, taking 1 from a2 each time (addi a2, a2, -1), until a2 is zero (beq a2, x0, done).
rv.hint.fib: Keep the last two numbers in a0 and t1 (start with 0 and 1). Each turn: t2 = a0 + t1, then a0 = t1, then t1 = t2, and take 1 from a1.
rv.hint.fast: 1 + 2 + … + n is n × (n + 1) ÷ 2. Add 1 to a1, multiply (mul), then halve with a shift to the right (srli).
rv.done: Three programs on an open processor. Every app, game and AI model is made of steps like these, only billions of them a second, on cores like this one copied many times.
rv.note: The lab's RISC-V simulator (RV32I, the integer instructions, and the M extension for the last puzzle), from the first site's RISC-V lab. One instruction takes one cycle here; a real core overlaps several at once.
srch.intro: One circuit, made two ways. A person designed it with care: that is the flat line. A blind search changes a circuit at random, checks it on the inputs, and keeps the change if it is no worse. Give the search more circuits to try, and watch where it passes the person.
srch.aria: Smallest working circuit found: {best} cells. The person's design: {hand} cells.
srch.legend: The line steps down each time the search finds a smaller circuit that passes the checker. A cell is one gate of the studio's library. The squares are the eight input patterns, for the best circuit within the budget: ✓ right, ✗ wrong.
srch.g.beat: Search beats the person, every input checked
srch.g.fooled: Checker tries half: search "wins", and is wrong
srch.msg.none: Within {b} circuits tried, nothing is right on every input checked yet. Spend more.
srch.msg.beat: Within {b} circuits tried, the search found a circuit of {c} cells, right on every input: smaller than the person's {h}.
srch.msg.tie: Within {b} circuits tried, the search matches the person: {c} cells. Spend more to see if it passes.
srch.msg.bigger: Within {b} circuits tried, the search's best is right but bigger than the person's: {c} cells against {h}. Spend more.
srch.msg.fooled: The checker passed a circuit of {c} cells, far smaller than the person's {h}. On all {n} inputs it is right on only {r}: it learned the test, not the job.
srch.msg.wrong: The checker passed a circuit of {c} cells that is right on only {r} of the {n} inputs, though not yet smaller than the person's {h}.
srch.msg.lucky: The checker passed a circuit of {c} cells, and by luck it is right on every input, even those never tried.
srch.hint.beat: Keep the voter and every input, and raise the computing until the line drops under the person's. A wider circuit needs far more.
srch.hint.fooled: Now let the checker try only half the inputs, and look at the squares under the curve.
srch.done: Both seen. More computing wins where every answer can be checked; where the checker sees only part, the search wins the test and fails the job. What can be checked, and by whom?
srch.note: From Rich Sutton's essay The Bitter Lesson (2019, incompleteideas.net). The search is the lab's evolve engine (Cartesian genetic programming, Miller and Thomson, 2000): each round it tries four changed copies of the best circuit. Size is counted in cells after the studio's synthesis, for the person's design and the search's alike. One run is one seed: another run may cross earlier or later.
halt.intro1: A gate is a tiny decision: two inputs in, one output out. Pick a material, then make the output go off only when both A and B are on. Tap A and B to try them.
halt.intro2: An agent claims it can tell whether any program stops. Its method: run the program for a budget of steps. If it has stopped, it says "stops"; if not, it guesses "never stops". Build programs from blocks, run them on the community's RISC-V core, and prove it wrong.
halt.g.aria: A gate made of {m}: A is {a}, B is {b}, the output is {o}.
halt.out.water.follow: the cup fills from the pipe
halt.out.domino.follow: the row topples the last domino
halt.out.domino.invert: the row breaks a second row
halt.cap.water.follow: A tank on the left. Water reaches the cup only through open valves.
halt.cap.water.invert: A second tank keeps the cup full; water that gets through the valves drains it away.
halt.cap.light.follow: A lamp on the left. Its light reaches the output only through open shutters.
halt.cap.light.invert: A second lamp lights the output; light that gets through the shutters closes a shade in front of it.
halt.cap.domino.follow: A push on the left. The row topples through a gap only where a domino stands in it.
halt.cap.domino.invert: A second row topples down to the output; a row that gets through the gaps knocks a domino out of it first, and the output stays standing.
halt.msg.and: Yours is on only when both are on: an AND gate. Close, but the wanted output is the other way round.
halt.msg.or: Yours is on when either is on: an OR gate. Not yet.
halt.msg.nor: Yours is off when either is on: a NOR gate. Almost: the wanted one is off only when both are on.
halt.msg.nand: That is a NAND gate: off only when both are on. From this one kind of gate every other can be built, in any material.
halt.l.aria: Two gates, each feeding the other. The bit holds {q}.
halt.l.notfed: not fed back: each gate only answers its own push
halt.l.cap: Two of your gates. Push Set or Reset: without feedback, the bit falls back as soon as you let go.
halt.l.capFed: Each gate's output now feeds the other's input, so each holds the other where it is after the push is gone.
halt.ui.fed: Feed each output back into the other gate
halt.push.set.0: While you pushed, the bit showed 1. You let go, and it fell back to 0: it forgot.
halt.push.reset.0: The bit shows 0. Without feedback it is always back to 0 once you let go, so it remembers nothing.
halt.push.set.1f: Pushed and let go: the bit still shows 1. The two gates hold each other: it remembers.
halt.push.reset.0f: Reset and let go: the bit shows 0 and stays 0. A bit that holds either way is memory.
halt.pattern: A processor is a very large number of such gates in a pattern. Silicon is only the material that makes them small, fast and cheap: a computer is a pattern, not a material.
halt.ui.deeper: Go deeper: the program nobody can judge
halt.hint.gate: The output should be off in one row only: when both are on. Try one after the other, with an output that is on unless something gets through.
halt.hint.bit: Feed each output back, then push Set, then push Reset.
halt.note1: Teaching models of the pattern, not working machines: domino, water and light gates have been built, but real ones need care with timing, and with a signal that grows weaker at every step.
halt.r.empty: no blocks: it stops at once
halt.r.press: Run the program to see both.
halt.r.cap: Both lanes count steps on one scale, ten times more at each mark. The agent stops looking at its budget; the program goes on to its end, or forever.
halt.blk.ask: ask the agent about this program, do the opposite
halt.msg2.stops: It stopped within the budget, and the agent saw it: right.
halt.msg2.never: It never stops, and the agent guessed so: right, this time.
halt.msg2.fooled: The agent gave up at {b} steps and guessed "never". The program stopped after {n}: fooled. A bigger budget only moves the wall.
halt.msg2.self: To answer, the agent must run this very program, which first asks the agent again, so its answer never comes within its budget. It guesses "never", and the program, told so, stops. Whatever the budget, whatever the method: fooled.
halt.open.k: What else is in this class
halt.open.p1: No program can tell, for every program, whether it stops. The same holds for any question about what a program does, rather than how it is written (Rice, 1953): whether it ever crashes, leaks a secret, or computes what its maker meant.
halt.open.p2: So no checker can be sure of every design an AI hands it. What can be done: check designs small or regular enough to bound, prove properties of the ones built to be proved, and test the rest. When a system is too complex to inspect, what can trust rest on?
halt.hint.fool: Make the program count to more steps than the agent's budget, and then stop.
halt.hint.more: Give the agent a bigger budget, then count higher than that.
halt.hint.self: Clear the program and use the last block: ask the agent about this very program, and do the opposite.
halt.done: All three fooled. However large the budget, however clever the agent, the program built on it proves it wrong: Turing's argument of 1936.
halt.note2: Turing, On computable numbers (1936, doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.230); Rice's theorem (1953). The blocks become RISC-V instructions on the lab's simulator, and the ask is one call the lab answers. This agent only runs and guesses; Turing's proof covers any method at all.
